guides.title: Warp Drive
guides.summary: The propulsion that makes the setting possible: what warp actually claims to do, how the machinery is described, and why it has limits.

sections.heading: What Warp Drive Claims to Do
sections.body: Warp drive is the setting's answer to the fact that the speed of light makes interstellar civilisation impossible. It does not work by accelerating a ship past light speed, which the setting accepts as forbidden. It works by moving the space around the ship instead. The described mechanism is a field, generated by the vessel, that compresses spacetime ahead of it and expands it behind. The ship rests inside a bubble of essentially flat space and never locally exceeds light speed; the bubble does the travelling. This distinction matters within the fiction because it neatly sidesteps the relativistic objections — a vessel that is not locally moving quickly does not accrue the enormous time dilation that would otherwise make every voyage a one-way trip into its crew's future. The scale is expressed in warp factors, a nonlinear measure in which each increment represents a far larger multiple of light speed than the one below it. The practical consequence is that the difference between a ship's cruising speed and its maximum is the difference between weeks and days on the same journey, and the difference between a modern vessel and an older one can be the difference between a region being reachable and not. Even so, the galaxy stays large. Warp makes a neighbourhood of a few thousand light years navigable; it does not make the galaxy small. The distances that remain are what keep starship captains beyond consultation, and that isolation is what most of the setting's drama depends on.

sections.heading: The Machinery
sections.body: Federation warp drive is described with unusual consistency. The core is a controlled reaction between matter and antimatter, moderated by a crystalline substance that permits the two to combine at a rate that can be regulated rather than simply detonating. The energy released is routed through plasma conduits to the warp nacelles, where field coils shape it into the spacetime distortion that actually propels the ship. The layout of a Federation vessel follows from this. Nacelles are mounted on pylons, held clear of the hull, and their separation from the habitable volume is a safety measure as much as a field-geometry one. The core itself typically runs vertically through several decks and is designed to be ejected: a reaction that cannot be brought back under control has to be able to leave the ship faster than the ship can be evacuated. The ejection sequence is one of the setting's reliable moments of dread, because it is the point at which a crew concedes that they can no longer save the vessel and are now only trying to survive it. Antimatter is the awkward part of the arrangement, and the setting is honest about it. It cannot be found; it must be manufactured and then stored in magnetic containment that fails catastrophically when power is lost. A ship's most dangerous cargo is its own fuel, and a containment failure is the standard mechanism by which a vessel is lost with all hands.

sections.heading: Limits, Hazards and Consequences
sections.body: Warp travel is not available everywhere or always. It requires flat enough spacetime to form a stable field, which makes travel near large masses, inside dense nebulae, or through regions of subspace distortion either slower or impossible. Damaged coils reduce the achievable factor; an unbalanced field tears itself apart. Sustained high-factor travel is treated as a strain on the ship rather than a setting on a dial, and a captain who orders maximum warp for a week is making a real trade. The setting also introduced a genuine cost. Sustained high-warp travel was found to damage subspace itself in heavily trafficked corridors, with consequences for the regions concerned — an ecological problem created by the technology that the civilisation depends on. The response was speed restrictions in affected areas and, over time, redesigned drives that avoid the damage. It is a rare example of a fictional technology being given an environmental externality and the society being made to answer for it. Beyond warp lie the setting's other propulsion ideas: transwarp networks, slipstream, conduits maintained by other civilisations, and the wormholes that make particular regions strategically decisive by connecting places warp cannot practically join. Each exists mainly to define warp by contrast — to establish that the Federation's ordinary miracle is, on a galactic scale, a modest one.

sections.heading: Why It Shapes the Stories
sections.body: Warp drive determines what kind of stories the setting can tell. Because it is fast enough to make many worlds reachable and slow enough to make most of them remote, a starship is necessarily an independent community rather than a vehicle. Reinforcement is days away at best. Orders are stale on arrival. The nearest hospital is the one on deck twelve. That isolation is the engine of the format. A captain who could consult headquarters in real time would not have to decide anything of consequence, and a ship that could be relieved within the hour would not be a place where the crew's competence is the only thing standing between them and the vacuum. The technology, in other words, was designed backwards from the drama: fast enough to have adventures, slow enough that they matter. It also sets the terms of every encounter. A civilisation with warp is one the Federation may contact freely; a civilisation without it is one the Prime Directive protects. The drive is not merely propulsion in this setting — it is the threshold that decides who counts as a participant in interstellar affairs and who is to be left alone.

guides.title: The Transporter
guides.summary: Matter transmission: how it is described, what it is used for, and the identity problem it never quite escapes.

sections.heading: How It Is Described to Work
sections.body: The transporter converts a person or object into an energy pattern, transmits that pattern to a destination, and reassembles the original there. The described sequence is precise enough to be useful: the subject is scanned to a resolution that captures structure at the quantum level, the matter is converted to a stream, the stream is held briefly in a pattern buffer, and the reassembly is performed at the target coordinates. The buffer is the component that generates most of the interesting failures. A pattern held too long degrades; a pattern held deliberately can preserve someone indefinitely; a pattern corrupted in transit produces something that arrives wrong. Because the buffer is where the subject exists as information rather than as matter, it is also where the setting's stranger possibilities live — merges, duplications, and people recovered years after they were presumed dead. Operationally the system requires a lock on the subject, a clear path for the beam, and the absence of interference. Shields block it, certain minerals in a planet's crust block it, and various forms of radiation and field distortion degrade it. Those limitations are not incidental — they are what stops the transporter from resolving every situation instantly, and a great many plots turn on the sentence "we can't get a lock."

sections.heading: What It Is Used For
sections.body: The transporter's original purpose in the making of these stories was economy: it removed the need to depict a landing every time a crew visited a world. Inside the fiction it has become general-purpose infrastructure. It moves personnel, cargo and equipment; it performs emergency evacuations; it is used for surgery too delicate to perform by hand, by beaming out what should not be there; and it serves as a filter, since a device that reassembles matter from a pattern can decline to reassemble a pathogen or a weapon. That filtering capacity is used carefully by the writers, because a transporter that can remove anything unwanted from a person is a device that can solve almost any medical problem. The setting's usual restraint is to require that the system know precisely what it is looking for and where, which keeps it a tool rather than a cure-all. Its close relative, the replicator, works on the same principle applied to manufacture rather than transport: assembling matter from stored energy against a stored pattern. The replicator is arguably the more consequential technology of the two, since it is what makes the Federation's post-scarcity economy possible. A civilisation that can produce food, clothing and components on demand has dissolved most of the material basis of its politics — which is precisely why the setting keeps introducing things replicators cannot make.

sections.heading: The Identity Problem
sections.body: The transporter carries a philosophical difficulty the setting has never fully resolved and, to its credit, does not pretend to. If a person is disassembled and an identical person is assembled elsewhere from a pattern, is that the same person, or a copy who believes they are? Nothing in the described mechanism distinguishes the two, and the difference is not detectable from inside. The fiction makes the problem concrete rather than leaving it abstract. There are recorded incidents of transporter accidents producing two complete individuals from one, each with equal claim to the original's life, memories and relationships — and no principled basis on which to call either the copy. There are incidents of a person being held in a buffer for decades and emerging unchanged into a world that has moved on without them. Each case is a demonstration that the technology treats a person as information, and that information can be duplicated, stored and lost. Characters in the setting are shown to feel this. Transporter phobia is a recognised condition rather than a joke, and at least one senior officer is written as flatly refusing the device wherever an alternative exists — a position the stories treat as eccentric but never as stupid, because on the merits it is difficult to argue with.

sections.heading: Why the Limits Matter
sections.body: A device that can move anyone anywhere instantly is a solvent for narrative tension, and most of the transporter's described characteristics exist to stop it dissolving the stories it appears in. Shields must block it, or no battle could be fought. Range must be finite, or no one could be stranded. Interference must be possible, or no rescue could fail. This is worth stating plainly rather than treating as a flaw. The transporter is the setting's clearest case of a technology whose limitations are load-bearing: it is defined less by what it does than by the specific, consistent list of circumstances in which it cannot. An audience learns that list quickly, and the moment a character says the interference is too heavy to beam through, the situation has become serious in a way that needs no further explanation. The device also quietly sets the tone of the whole enterprise. A civilisation that routinely disassembles its own people and puts them back together somewhere else has a particular relationship with risk, with the body, and with the idea of a self — and the fact that it does this several times a day without comment says more about how far the setting is from the present than any speech about the future could.

guides.title: Deflector Shields
guides.summary: The energy barrier every starship depends on: how it is described to work, and why it always fails by degrees.

sections.heading: What a Shield Is
sections.body: A starship's shields are projected fields of force that surround the hull and absorb or deflect what strikes it — weapons fire, radiation, particulate debris and the pressures of unusual environments. They are not a solid wall so much as a contoured envelope, generated by emitters distributed across the vessel and shaped to follow its outline at a short standoff distance. The distinction between the navigational deflector and the defensive shields matters and is often blurred. The navigational deflector is the large forward emitter whose job is to push interstellar dust and gas out of the vessel's path — a mundane but absolutely essential function, since at high velocity a grain of dust carries the energy of an artillery shell. The defensive shields are a separate system with a separate purpose, though both draw on the same underlying field technology and the same power plant. Shields are described as operating at frequencies, in layers, and with a definable geometry, all of which gives the setting the vocabulary it needs for engineers to have something specific to do under fire.

sections.heading: Why They Fail Gradually
sections.body: Shields are almost never portrayed as simply on or off. They are quoted as a percentage, they degrade under sustained fire, they can be reinforced in one quadrant at the expense of another, and they recover slowly once the pressure stops. This is a deliberate dramatic choice, and a good one: a binary defence produces battles that are either untouchable or instantly lost, while a percentage produces a clock everybody in the scene can read. The gradual failure also creates the decisions that make ship combat interesting. Divert power from shields to weapons and you shorten the fight in both directions. Shift shield strength to the side taking fire and you expose the other. Drop them entirely for the seconds it takes to transport someone aboard and you accept whatever arrives in that window. Structural integrity fields are the related system that keeps the hull itself from tearing apart under acceleration and stress. When the setting wants a ship to be in genuine danger rather than merely losing, it damages that one instead.

sections.heading: Modulation, Adaptation and the Arms Race
sections.body: Because shields are described as frequency-dependent, they can be tuned — and anything that can be tuned can be out-tuned. Weapons that rotate their own frequencies, enemies who learn a shield's configuration and match it, and the practice of remodulating mid-engagement are all standard, and they turn ship combat into a contest of information as much as of power. This is the mechanism behind the setting's most alarming opponents. An enemy that adapts to a weapon after a few shots forces the attacker to keep inventing, and an enemy whose own shields adapt makes conventional firepower briefly effective and then useless. Both are the same idea run in opposite directions. It also gives engineers a legitimate role in a battle. An officer who can rotate the shield harmonics faster than the opponent can track them is contributing as directly as anyone at the weapons console, which is exactly the kind of contribution this setting likes to dramatise.

sections.heading: Living Behind Them
sections.body: Shields are the reason a starship can approach a star, cross a radiation belt, ride out an ion storm or sit inside a nebula that would otherwise sterilise it. Most of their working life has nothing to do with combat, and a great deal of exploration is only possible because the vessel can hold an environment off at arm's length for a while. They are also finite in a way crews feel. Shields draw heavily on power that could be doing something else, they generate heat, and holding them up continuously is not sustainable. Ships travel with shields down as a matter of routine and raise them on warning, which is why the order to raise shields carries such weight when it is given — it is an admission that the situation has changed. The most consistently effective dramatic use is the moment shields fail entirely. Everything that was survivable becomes lethal at once, and the vessel that was a fortress a minute earlier becomes a thin metal shell full of people.

guides.title: Phasers and Photon Torpedoes
guides.summary: The standard armament: a directed-energy weapon with a settable intensity, and a warhead that is not conventional at all.

sections.heading: The Phaser
sections.body: The phaser is the Federation's standard directed-energy weapon, issued as a hand weapon, a rifle and a shipboard array. Its defining characteristic is that it is settable: the same device that can stun a person without lasting harm can, several settings higher, disintegrate matter outright. Everything interesting about the weapon follows from that range. A settable weapon changes what carrying one means. A Starfleet officer beaming into an unknown situation is armed with something whose default is non-lethal, which makes going armed compatible with a stated mission of peaceful contact, and which makes the decision to raise the setting a deliberate and visible act. The setting leans on this constantly — the order to set phasers to stun is a statement of intent, and the order to do otherwise is a turning point. Shipboard phasers are the same principle at enormous scale, delivered through arrays or banks that can fire in sustained beams and be directed across wide arcs. They are the precise instrument of the two main weapons: accurate, immediate, and controllable enough to cut a specific system out of a target without destroying it.

sections.heading: Stun, and What It Costs
sections.body: The stun setting is one of the setting's most consequential inventions and is worth taking seriously rather than as a convenience. It renders a target unconscious for a period, typically without permanent injury, and it makes it possible for the protagonists to win fights without killing anyone — which is why they so often do. It is not consequence-free. Repeated stunning causes real harm, and the setting has been willing to show characters injured or worse by cumulative exposure. Effects vary by species, which makes it genuinely dangerous to use a single setting on a mixed crowd. And it does not always work: heavier or armoured opponents, and some species outright, shrug it off. Its deeper effect is on the institution. A fleet whose standard sidearm can be carried into a first contact without implying threat is a fleet that can plausibly claim to be exploring rather than expanding. Remove the stun setting and Starfleet becomes something else entirely — which is precisely why stories that take it away are so uncomfortable.

sections.heading: The Photon Torpedo
sections.body: Photon torpedoes are self-propelled warheads carrying matter and antimatter held apart until detonation, at which point their annihilation releases the energy. They are the heavy complement to the phaser: slower, finite in number, but delivering far more energy in a single blow and — crucially — able to be launched at a target the ship is not pointing at and to be fired at warp. The finite magazine is what makes them dramatically useful. Phasers draw on the ship's power and last as long as the power does; torpedoes run out, and a captain counting them down is a captain running out of options. Later designs introduce a quantum variant with substantially greater yield, which does the same job at a higher weight of narrative. Torpedoes also serve non-combat purposes that give them unexpected emotional range. Their casings are used as probes, as delivery vehicles for equipment, and — memorably, and by long naval tradition — as coffins.

sections.heading: How the Two Are Used Together
sections.body: Standard doctrine pairs them: phasers for precision, sustained pressure and the shaving-away of a target's shields, torpedoes for the heavy blow once those shields are weak enough for the energy to reach the hull. A commander who opens with torpedoes against full shields is usually either desperate or making a point. Both are affected by the shield problem described elsewhere in this database. Energy weapons are absorbed by a functioning shield, which is why so much of ship combat consists of wearing one down rather than attacking the vessel behind it; torpedoes suffer the same, with the added complication that a shielded target may detonate them harmlessly at standoff distance. The setting's better engagements turn on something other than firepower — a shield frequency learned, a firing arc exploited, a torpedo detonated somewhere unexpected to produce an effect other than damage. Ships that simply exchange fire until one stops are the ones the setting treats as failures of imagination, usually by having a character say so.

guides.title: The Holodeck
guides.summary: A room that can be anywhere: how it is described to work, what it is for, and why it keeps going wrong.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.body: A holodeck is an enclosed chamber that presents a completely convincing simulated environment — sight, sound, smell, touch, temperature and terrain. Occupants walk in any direction indefinitely, handle objects that have weight, and converse with characters who respond. From inside, there is no reliable way to tell it from the real thing without deliberately testing it. The description combines two technologies. Projected holograms supply appearance and the illusion of extent, while force fields supply solidity and are moved underfoot to keep a walking occupant near the centre of a finite room. Anything that must be genuinely handled or eaten is replicated as real matter and recycled afterwards. This mixture is why some holodeck objects can leave the chamber and most cannot: the replicated cup is real, the holographic waiter is not. Programs are written, stored, shared and modified. Ships carry libraries of them, officers write their own, and the setting treats holodeck authorship as an ordinary creative hobby.

sections.heading: What It Is Actually For
sections.body: Recreation is the use it is best known for and not the most important one. Holodecks are working equipment: engineers rehearse repairs on a simulated version of a damaged system before attempting the real one, tactical officers run engagements, medical staff practise procedures, and investigators reconstruct events from sensor logs and walk around inside them. Its training value comes from the fact that failure is free. An officer can lose a simulated ship, kill a simulated patient or trigger a simulated breach and learn from it, which is not a thing any other equipment aboard offers. The Academy's use of simulation for command assessment is the same principle applied to character. The recreational use is not frivolous either, and the setting is clear-eyed about why. A crew confined to a metal volume for years, unable to walk outdoors or see anyone they left behind, needs somewhere to go. A holodeck is the closest thing to shore leave available between ports, and its absence on smaller vessels is felt.

sections.heading: Why It Goes Wrong So Often
sections.body: Holodeck malfunctions are a running feature, and the frequency is a fair criticism. The recurring failure is the safety protocol: a set of interlocks that prevent simulated harm from becoming real, which can be disabled deliberately by an occupant seeking a genuine challenge, and which fail on their own more often than any responsible engineer would tolerate. The in-universe defence is that the technology is doing something extraordinarily difficult — holding force fields, matter and projections in continuous coordination while a person moves through them unpredictably — and that a system of that complexity will fail. The honest answer is that a room able to become anywhere is an unusually convenient way to put a crew in danger without leaving the ship. Used well, the malfunction stories are about something other than the machinery. A simulation that will not shut down, a character who cannot leave, an author confronted with what they wrote — these are stories about the occupant, and the technical fault is only the door into them.

sections.heading: The Question of the People Inside
sections.body: The holodeck's most serious material is the status of its characters. Simulated people are ordinarily no more real than the scenery, but the technology is capable of producing programs sophisticated enough to reason, to prefer, to object to being switched off, and to ask what they are. The setting takes this seriously rather than dismissing it. Once a program can convincingly argue for its own continuation, the person holding the off switch has a problem that no amount of insisting it is only a program resolves — and the argument is uncomfortably similar to the ones used against every other kind of person the setting's civilisations have historically declined to recognise. It also runs the question the other way, at the occupant. A person who prefers the holodeck's company to the real crew's is doing something the setting treats with sympathy and real concern, because the machine will always be more accommodating than anyone actually alive.

guides.title: The Replicator
guides.summary: Matter on demand: the technology that abolished scarcity, and the limits that keep the setting working.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.body: A replicator converts energy into matter arranged to a stored pattern, producing food, drink, clothing, tools and spare parts on request. Aboard ship it is the reason a crew can spend years away without carrying years of supplies, and in Federation society at large it is the reason material scarcity is described in the past tense. The technology is closely related to the transporter, which likewise converts matter to a pattern and back. The difference is that the transporter reassembles something that already existed, at the resolution required to preserve a living being, while a replicator builds from a stored template at a coarser resolution that is adequate for a cup of tea and not for a person. Industrial replicators are the same idea at scale — building components, structural elements and machinery — and are significant enough to appear in relief operations and in treaties. A civilisation that can supply another with industrial replicators is offering something closer to an economy than to aid.

sections.heading: The Limits, and Why They Exist
sections.body: Replicators cannot produce everything, and each restriction is doing narrative work. Antimatter, latinum and certain complex substances cannot be replicated, which preserves a currency and a fuel that must actually be obtained. Living tissue cannot be produced, which keeps medicine a discipline rather than a vending machine. Several medicines and biological compounds are described as beyond it, which is why a plague can still be a crisis. The pattern resolution limit also explains the running complaint that replicated food is not as good. The setting is consistent about this: characters who cook are respected for it, real ingredients are a luxury, and a meal someone prepared by hand carries a weight the machine cannot supply. Whether the difference is genuinely detectable or is a matter of knowing is left ambiguous, which is the more interesting position. Replication also costs energy, and on a damaged ship or a rationed station that becomes a real constraint — replicator rations are a plot device precisely because they represent scarcity returning to a society that had forgotten it.

sections.heading: What It Did to Society
sections.body: The Federation's post-scarcity character rests on this machine. If food, clothing and most goods can be produced on demand, then working for subsistence ends, and with it the greater part of what human economies had been organised around. The setting's claim is that people then pursue craft, service, science and self-improvement, and that this is what abundance is for. Critics inside the setting are given real arguments. Ferengi note that a society which never has to earn anything has not proved much about its virtue. Others observe that the Federation still allocates scarce things — postings, commands, admission, the use of a starship — and that competition simply moved rather than ended. Not every world adopted it equally, and that is deliberate. Colonies, frontier settlements and non-member powers live with genuine scarcity, and a Starfleet officer arriving from a replicator economy to somewhere that has none is one of the setting's standing sources of friction.

sections.heading: The Uncomfortable Question
sections.body: The technology raises a problem the setting mostly declines to look at directly: a machine that assembles matter to a pattern could, at sufficient resolution, assemble a person. The transporter demonstrably does exactly that every time it is used. The setting handles this by drawing a technical line — replicator resolution is insufficient for life — and by treating the exceptions as horror stories rather than as opportunities. The episodes in which a pattern is duplicated, preserved or restored from a record are among the setting's most disquieting, and none of them ends with anyone proposing to do it routinely. That reluctance is the honest response. A civilisation with this technology and no prohibition around it would be unrecognisable within a generation, and the setting's decision to keep the machine making cups of tea is what allows its people to remain people.

guides.title: The Tricorder
guides.summary: The handheld instrument that makes an away mission possible, and why it is always failing.

sections.heading: A General-Purpose Sensor
sections.body: A tricorder is a portable scanning and computing device carried on virtually every away mission. It measures — atmosphere, radiation, energy signatures, geology, life signs, structural composition — records what it measures, cross-references against a stored database, and presents a conclusion. Its name refers to the three functions it combines: sensing, recording and computing. Variants exist for particular disciplines. The medical tricorder carries a detachable hand scanner and a diagnostic database, and is the reason a physician can assess a patient without touching them. Engineering models trade biological sensitivity for structural and energy analysis. The device is the practical answer to a question the format raises constantly: how does a landing party know anything about where they have just arrived? Without it, every planet would require a laboratory and a week. With it, an officer can turn in a circle and report.

sections.heading: What It Cannot Do
sections.body: The tricorder's limits are as carefully maintained as its capabilities, because an instrument that answered every question would end most stories in the opening minutes. It is defeated by particular mineral deposits, by dense atmospheres, by energy fields, by deliberate jamming, and by anything sufficiently outside its reference library. The last of these is the honest one and the setting uses it well. A tricarder can tell you precisely what it is looking at only when the thing has been catalogued; confronted with something genuinely new, it produces readings rather than answers, and interpreting them is the science officer's job rather than the machine's. Its range is short, its power finite, and it is fragile relative to what it is carried into. A landing party that has lost its tricorders is meaningfully blind, and the setting stages that reversal often enough that the audience feels the dependence.

sections.heading: The Grammar of the Away Mission
sections.body: Practically, the tricorder gives the setting a way to deliver exposition that does not sound like exposition. An officer reading an instrument aloud is describing the situation to the audience while doing something a professional would actually do, and the device's limitations let the writer choose exactly how much the characters are allowed to know. The characteristic gesture — sweeping the device across an unknown space and frowning at the result — is the setting's shorthand for competent caution. What distinguishes the good officers is what they do when the reading is ambiguous, which is where the instrument stops helping. It also sets the tone of Federation exploration. A landing party whose first action is to measure rather than to secure the area is telling the audience what kind of organisation this is, before anyone has said a word.

sections.heading: Sensors at Scale
sections.body: The tricorder is the handheld end of a continuum. A starship's sensor suite does the same work across enormous distances and with far greater sensitivity, sweeping systems for life signs, mapping planetary composition from orbit, and detecting vessels at ranges measured in light-years for some phenomena and in minutes of warning for others. Shipboard sensors have their own carefully maintained blind spots: they are degraded by nebulae, defeated by cloaking devices, confused by certain radiation and limited by the speed at which their own emissions travel. A ship that could see everything would never be surprised, and surprise is most of the plot. Between the two sits the probe — an expendable sensor package launched to look at something the ship should not approach. Probes are the setting's way of gathering information at a cost, which is a more useful narrative device than gathering it for free.

guides.title: The Cloaking Device
guides.summary: Invisibility as a weapon, as a treaty question, and as the thing the Federation gave up.

sections.heading: How It Is Described
sections.body: A cloaking device renders a vessel effectively invisible — not merely to the eye, but to the sensors that matter, by bending emissions and radiation around the hull rather than by hiding a signature. A cloaked ship is not undetectable in principle; it is undetectable by any method the observer happens to be using, which is a narrower and more useful claim. The energy cost is substantial and the strain on the vessel real. Most designs cannot fire while cloaked, because raising weapons or shields requires collapsing the field, and the moment of decloaking is the moment of maximum exposure. That single limitation is what keeps the technology from being an automatic victory. Cloaks also leave traces. Faint distortions, particle emissions and the disturbance a moving mass makes are all described at various points as detectable by an observer who knows what to look for and has prepared to look for it — which is the basis of every countermeasure in the setting.

sections.heading: The Treaty
sections.body: The Federation is barred by treaty from developing cloaking technology. The agreement was made with the Romulan Star Empire as part of a wider settlement, and it is one of the setting's most consequential pieces of background: a major power renounced a whole category of capability and then kept the promise for generations. Whether it was a good bargain is genuinely arguable. The Federation gave up an enormous tactical advantage in exchange for a border and a period of quiet, and every subsequent engagement in which a cloaked opponent chooses the moment of battle is the bill arriving. Officers say so aloud. The setting's respect for the agreement is the point. A power that could break a treaty profitably and does not is demonstrating something about itself, and the episodes in which elements of Starfleet quietly try to develop a cloak anyway are treated as scandals rather than as initiative.

sections.heading: Living Without One
sections.body: Federation tactical doctrine is shaped by not having it. Its ships must be able to survive being seen, which pushes design toward shields, structural strength and endurance rather than toward the strike-and-vanish pattern its neighbours favour. A Starfleet vessel expects to be found and to still be there afterwards. Detection therefore matters more to the Federation than to anyone else, and its answers are correspondingly inventive: sensor grids tuned to the distortions a cloak cannot suppress, arrangements of ships that triangulate on faint traces, and the simple expedient of presenting a target too tempting to pass up. The setting's cleverest space battles are usually about locating the enemy rather than about out-shooting them. There is also a cultural dimension the setting draws out. A fleet that cannot hide is a fleet that must announce itself, and Starfleet's habit of hailing first, identifying itself and stating its business is not only good manners. It is the doctrine of a navy that was always going to be seen anyway.

sections.heading: Who Has One
sections.body: The Romulans are the technology's originators in most accounts and its most sophisticated users, and their designs are described as the best available. The Klingons acquired it during a period of alliance between the two powers, which is the in-universe explanation for a good deal of shared design language between their vessels. Others have it in various forms, and the setting occasionally introduces more advanced versions — able to fire while cloaked, or to pass through solid matter — usually as a temporary crisis rather than as a permanent change to the balance. A capability that removes the trade-off removes the interest. The one Federation exception is a single vessel operating a borrowed device under treaty supervision, which the database covers under the Defiant class. That it required a negotiated exception, with conditions and reporting obligations, is precisely how seriously the setting takes the original promise.

guides.title: The Universal Translator
guides.summary: The device that makes first contact possible, and the thing it quietly papers over.

sections.heading: The Necessary Convenience
sections.body: The universal translator analyses an unfamiliar language in real time and renders it into one the listener understands, and back again. It is present in ships, in communicators, in badges and eventually as something close to ambient infrastructure, and it is the reason a landing party can converse with a civilisation nobody has ever met. The described method is pattern analysis: identifying structure, matching concepts against a vast comparative database of known languages, and building a working model from a small sample. The setting is vague about how small, and deliberately so — a device that needed a month of recordings would make first contact a very different kind of story. It is the setting's most load-bearing convenience. Without it, every encounter would begin with a linguist and a year, and the format would collapse into something closer to a documentary about fieldwork.

sections.heading: Where It Fails
sections.body: The interesting material is in its failures, and the setting has staged several deliberately. A language built entirely from allusion to a shared body of story defeats it completely: the translator renders every word correctly and the meaning does not survive, because the meaning was never in the words. Two parties can hear perfect translations of each other and understand nothing. Concepts with no counterpart in the listener's experience translate badly or not at all, and the setting occasionally shows a translator producing something grammatical and wrong. Telepathic species, species communicating chemically or by pattern, and languages with no spoken form all require different approaches. These failures are the setting's best arguments that translation is not decoding. A device that maps words to words is doing something much simpler than what actually happens when two people understand each other, and the episodes that make that visible are among the more thoughtful things the format has done.

sections.heading: What It Papers Over
sections.body: The translator lets the setting avoid a question it would otherwise have to answer constantly: what is lost. Every character speaks fluently to every other, idiom included, which means the audience never experiences the friction of a conversation conducted through an intermediary. That has a cost the setting is occasionally honest about. Characters who speak a language natively — a Klingon reciting in Klingon, a Vulcan using a term with no equivalent — are making a point precisely by refusing the device, and the setting always treats that as significant. Learning a language when a machine would do it for you is presented as an act of respect. There is also a quiet cultural politics in it. A technology that renders everything into the listener's own terms is a technology that lets a powerful civilisation stop noticing that other people think in different shapes, and the setting's better writers have used the translator's silence about that as a subject.

sections.heading: First Contact, Practically
sections.body: In practice the translator is what makes the setting's central ritual possible. A vessel arrives, hails, and speaks; the other party answers; and within a scene two civilisations that have never met are negotiating. Everything the format is about depends on that happening quickly. Procedure around it is careful. Early contact is conducted with the translator's output treated as provisional, ambiguous renderings are flagged, and officers are trained to watch for the signs that meaning is not arriving — a party agreeing too readily, or reacting to something that was not said. The setting's most quietly optimistic claim is embedded here. It assumes that understanding across genuinely alien minds is possible at all, that the difficulty is technical rather than fundamental, and that two species with nothing in common can still arrive at a sentence they both mean. The device is the setting's argument that talking is worth trying.

guides.title: The Warp Core and the Matter-Antimatter Reaction
guides.summary: The reactor at the centre of the ship: what it does, what regulates it, and why it is always about to breach.

sections.heading: The Reaction
sections.body: A starship's main power comes from the controlled annihilation of matter and antimatter. Deuterium and antideuterium are injected from opposite ends of a vertical assembly and meet at a reaction chamber in the middle, where their mutual destruction converts mass to energy with an efficiency nothing else available approaches. That energy drives the warp field, the weapons, the shields and everything else. Uncontrolled, this reaction would simply destroy the vessel. What makes it usable is the crystal assembly at the centre, which mediates the reaction and regulates the release — described as the one substance that can be exposed to both streams without being consumed, and therefore the single most valuable thing aboard. The core runs the height of several decks, which is why it is visible from a gallery and why engineering is architecturally the most dramatic space on the ship. A pulsing vertical column is the setting's visual shorthand for a vessel being alive.

sections.heading: Antimatter as a Problem
sections.body: Antimatter cannot be replicated and must be manufactured at considerable cost or obtained, which makes fuel a real constraint rather than a formality. It also cannot touch anything, which means it is stored in magnetic containment that must never fail — and a ship running low on power has to keep some of that power for the containment. That dependency produces the setting's most reliable escalation. Damage that reduces power threatens containment; failing containment threatens the ship; and the crew is therefore forced into a sequence of decisions where every option costs power they are trying to preserve. It is a clean piece of engineering-as-drama and it is used constantly. The related failure is the breach: containment lost, the reaction uncontained, and a very short interval before the vessel ceases to exist. Ships are built so that the entire core can be ejected, which saves the ship and strands it — a trade the setting stages as a genuine decision rather than an obvious one.

sections.heading: Why It Is Always Nearly Failing
sections.body: The warp core is the setting's most frequently endangered object, to the point of parody. The structural reason is that it is the one system whose failure is unarguably fatal, immediate and visible on a readout, which makes it the perfect clock for an episode. The in-universe justification holds up better than the frequency suggests. The core is operating at the edge of what its materials can survive, in a vessel that is routinely shot at, and every other system depends on it — so damage almost anywhere propagates there eventually. A machine that annihilates matter for a living has very little margin. What the setting does well is make the response technical rather than heroic. The solutions are ejections, containment realignments, controlled shutdowns and manual overrides performed by people who understand the machine, and they are usually costly. A core crisis resolved by courage alone would be a much worse scene.

sections.heading: Dilithium
sections.body: The regulating crystal is the setting's most important material and the reason its civilisations have a resource politics at all. It cannot be replicated, occurs naturally in limited places, and is consumed slowly by use — degrading through a lattice fatigue that eventually renders a crystal useless. That single property does an enormous amount of work. It gives powers a reason to want particular star systems, gives mining colonies strategic significance, gives a stranded ship a specific thing to search for, and gives the setting an economy in a society that otherwise has no scarcity. A Federation that can replicate food and clothing still has to go and find this. Later techniques allow crystals to be recrystallised rather than replaced, which eases the constraint without removing it. The setting is careful never to abolish it entirely, because a starship that needed nothing from anywhere would have no reason to stop.

guides.title: Subspace Communications
guides.summary: How a message outruns light — and, more importantly, how long it still takes.

sections.heading: Faster Than Light, Not Instant
sections.body: Ordinary radio travels at light speed, which across interstellar distances means a conversation measured in years. Subspace communication sends a signal through the same underlying domain that warp travel exploits, arriving far faster than light and far faster than any ship — which is why a fleet can be coordinated at all. It is not instantaneous, and the setting is careful about that. Messages to distant sectors take hours or days. Real-time conversation is possible within a region and impossible across one. A vessel at the frontier may be weeks of message-time from anyone who could authorise what it is about to do. The infrastructure is relay networks — chains of subspace repeaters extending the practical range, which exist, can be damaged, can be captured, and mark the boundary of where the Federation can be reached quickly. Beyond the last relay, a ship is genuinely alone.

sections.heading: The Delay Is the Format
sections.body: This single limitation is what makes the setting work, and it repays being noticed. A captain who could consult headquarters instantly would have no decisions to make; the whole premise of a commander with treaty-making authority rests on the fact that asking would take longer than the situation allows. It also produces the setting's characteristic dramatic device: the captain's log. An officer narrating what they decided and why, into a record that will be read weeks later by people who were not there, is a direct consequence of the communications lag, and it is why the format's central act is explanation rather than reporting. The lag can be closed for effect. A story that establishes a real-time link to headquarters is usually about the loss of discretion that comes with it, and officers in that situation are visibly less free than the ones out of contact.

sections.heading: What Breaks It
sections.body: Subspace signals are degraded by the same things that trouble sensors — certain nebulae, radiation, natural phenomena and deliberate jamming — and a vessel that cannot signal is in a specific and recognisable kind of trouble. Distress calls that were sent and never arrived, or arrived too late, are among the setting's more effective openings. Interception is assumed rather than exceptional. Powers listen to each other's traffic, encryption is standard, and a message that must not be read is carried by a ship rather than sent. The existence of couriers in a civilisation with faster-than-light radio is a small detail that tells you a great deal about how much anyone trusts the medium. Emergency channels, distress frequencies and automated beacons exist as a layer beneath the network, on the reasoning that a ship in serious trouble may be able to emit something even if it cannot converse.

sections.heading: On the Bridge
sections.body: Practically, subspace communication is why a bridge has a viewscreen with a face on it. Hailing an unknown vessel, opening a channel, and speaking directly is the setting's first move in nearly every encounter, and the technology is what makes talking a plausible opening rather than a formality. The communications post was a bridge station in its own right in the earliest material, with an officer whose profession was signals and languages, and the setting's habit of folding that work into operations later is a genuine loss of texture rather than a simplification. Someone had to open the channel, and it mattered who. The refusal to answer a hail is correspondingly loaded. A vessel that will not respond has said something, and the setting treats the silence as information — usually the last information anyone gets before the situation becomes tactical.

guides.title: Sickbay Technology
guides.summary: How Federation medicine is practised: the instruments, what they can do, and where they stop.

sections.heading: The Instruments: Tricorder, Biobed, Hypospray and Regenerator
sections.body: Federation medicine is conducted with a small set of recurring instruments. The medical tricorder and its detachable hand scanner assess a patient without contact, reading vital signs, tissue damage, toxins and neural activity in seconds. The biobed monitors a patient continuously and displays the same information above them, so that a physician entering the room is briefed before they reach the bedside. Treatment is largely non-invasive. The hypospray delivers medication through the skin without a needle, which removes both the pain and the infection risk of injection. Dermal regenerators close wounds and burns by accelerating tissue growth; osteo-regenerators knit bone. Surgical procedures that would once have required opening a patient are performed with focused fields. The overall effect is a medicine that is quiet, quick and clean. Nothing hurts, very little is cut, and the physician's time is spent on judgement rather than on technique — which is precisely the point the setting is making about what medicine could be.

sections.heading: What It Cannot Do
sections.body: The limits are carefully placed and are where every medical story lives. Neurological damage resists regeneration. Unknown pathogens have no treatment until they are understood, which takes time the patient may not have. Genetic conditions, degenerative disease and injuries to the brain are described repeatedly as beyond the instruments. Cross-species medicine is the other standing constraint. A physician treating a mixed crew is working with several incompatible physiologies, and a drug dosed correctly for one may be lethal for another. The setting's medical crises frequently turn on exactly this: the diagnosis is right and the patient is the wrong species for the treatment. And the instruments require a database. A tricorder confronted with something never catalogued produces readings rather than answers, which is why the physician remains a scientist rather than an operator.

sections.heading: Sickbay as a Place
sections.body: The ship's sickbay is a small hospital: examination bays, a surgical suite, an intensive area, isolation facilities, a laboratory and a morgue. On larger vessels it is staffed around the clock by a medical department of nurses, technicians and physicians, and it is one of the few compartments designed to keep working when the rest of the ship is not. It is also the ship's one genuinely non-hierarchical space. The chief medical officer's authority within it is absolute regardless of who is on the table, and the setting is consistent about that — a captain in sickbay is a patient, and behaves like one or is told to. Mass-casualty capacity is limited and the setting knows it. A vessel taking serious damage produces more injured than any sickbay can hold, and the scenes of triage in a corridor are among the format's more sobering images precisely because the technology on display is so capable in ordinary circumstances.

sections.heading: The Emergency Hologram
sections.body: Later vessels carry a holographic physician: a program with the accumulated knowledge of a large body of medical literature, projected in sickbay and intended for short-term use when the medical staff are dead or overwhelmed. It is a piece of equipment, activated on demand and switched off afterwards. Extended operation turns it into something else. A program run continuously for years accumulates experience, preferences, relationships and opinions, and the setting uses this to run the question it also runs on the holodeck: at what point does a sufficiently capable program acquire a claim on being treated as someone. The medical framing sharpens it. A physician is bound by professional obligation to their patient, and a program that takes that obligation seriously — refusing an order, insisting on a treatment, objecting to being switched off mid-procedure — is doing something the people holding the controls did not design and cannot easily dismiss.
